body:
Porinju Veliyath started as a floor trader at Kotak in 1990, worked as an analyst at Parag Parikh Securities, and founded Equity Intelligence in Kochi in 2002 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porinju_Veliyath)). He runs concentrated portfolios of 10–12 mostly small and mid-cap stocks and charges a **2% fixed fee plus 10% of returns above a 10% hurdle** ([Equity Intelligence](https://www.equityintelligence.com/portfolio-management-service)). The firm's own numbers show both sides. FY14 returned +59%, FY15 +79% and FY21 +152%. **FY19 was −31.87% and FY20 −51.48%**, while the Nifty 50 TRI was +16.45% and −25.02% ([Equity Intelligence](https://www.equityintelligence.com/portfolio-management-service)). Compounded, those two years come to about −67%. An investor who entered at the FY18 peak was back to roughly breakeven only after FY22, four years in which the Nifty nearly doubled. The causes were partly his own. He publicly backed low-governance "chor" stocks for re-rating and later admitted the strategy "backfired" ([blog compilation of ET interviews](https://rakesh-jhunjhunwala.in/i-burnt-fingers-badly-with-chor-stocks-porinju-veliyath-concedes-defeat-vows-to-stay-away-from-chors-invest-only-in-cos-with-integrity/)). He held about 8% of LEEL Electricals, which collapsed. He alleged diversion of sale proceeds by the promoters and said "in hindsight it looks a mistake" ([Hans India](https://www.thehansindia.com/posts/index/Latest-News/2019-01-13/Made-a-mistake-says-Porinju-Veliyath-after-investor-wealth-eroded-by-44/474694)).

The "Porinju effect" is the trap for copycats. His bulk-deal buys often trigger upper circuits as retail investors pile in. BEML, for example, rose 51% in five weeks after his firm bought a stake ([Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/topic/porinju-veliyath)). Followers buy after the disclosure and the move, at worse prices, without his information or his exit timing. The only SEBI order naming him that this research found is a 2009 consent order in a Geojit Securities matter, whose terms could not be read ([SEBI](https://www.sebi.gov.in/enforcement/orders/sep-2009/consent-order-on-the-application-submitted-by-shri-porinju-veliyath-in-the-matter-of-geojit-securities-limited_3827.html)). No front-running or manipulation finding was found. There is also a business-model point: a 2% fixed fee keeps accruing in years when clients lose two-thirds.

body:
1. **Almost all stock-market wealth comes from very few stocks.** About 4% of US stocks
   created *all* the market's net wealth over 90 years. Most stocks lose to a bank FD.
   So we're hunting for rare winners, and most of our picks will be ordinary.
2. **F&O is a trap for individuals.** 88–93% of individual F&O traders in India lose
   money every year. In FY26, 82% were losing even *before* costs. Prop firms and
   foreign funds with algorithms took the other side. → **We don't do F&O.**
3. **Every legend had an unfair advantage, not just knowledge.**
   - Buffett: started at 11 in a market nobody studied; later used cheap insurance
     money (about 1.7x leverage); 99% of his wealth came after age 60–65.
   - Lynch: read ~700 annual reports and visited 200+ companies a year. Burned out at 46.
   - Damani: most of his wealth comes from *building* D-Mart, not trading.
   - Jhunjhunwala: started with "₹5,000" but borrowed his brother's clients' money; his
     biggest wealth came from a 1992 bet *against* the market; Titan was ~1/3 of his wealth.
4. **Myths we busted:** Titan wasn't bought at ₹3 (that's split-adjusted; he paid ₹30–50).
   The "Fidelity study of best investors being dead" never existed. Your Radico story
   was off: the 120 → 4,600 move started in **2016–17** (premium brands + debt falling),
   not from a 2008 UBL issue. UBL is a beer company.
5. **Multibaggers have "two engines":** profits grow *and* the market pays a higher P/E.
   Radico ≈ profit ×7.5 × P/E ×5 ≈ 38x.
6. **Winners fall hard along the way.** Amazon −94%, NVIDIA −50% twice, Radico −74%.
   You only get the reward if you can hold through that.
7. **Knowledge isn't the edge.** Millions read the same books. Edge = seeing what others
   don't, plus patience, plus never getting wiped out.
8. **AI doesn't pick winning stocks by itself.** AI trading contests mostly lost money;
   the oldest AI-run ETF trails the S&P 500. AI is great for *reading* and *checking*.
9. **Instant disqualifiers**, no matter how cheap the stock: promoter pledging shares,
   auditor qualifying the accounts, profits jumping with no real reason, growth funded
   by debt while cash flow is negative.
10. **Time and capital matter.** ₹25,000/month at 12% for 30 years ≈ ₹7.7 crore —
    more than ₹10,000/month at 15% (≈ ₹5.6 crore). Saving more beats chasing returns.

body: `insight:india-lead-indicator-dashboard` · confidence: single-source These free public series lead quarterly results, usually by 1–3 months. Autos: Vahan dashboard (daily registrations), FADA monthly retail and dealer inventory, SIAM monthly wholesales, tractor sales. Banks and NBFCs: RBI fortnightly credit and deposit data, RBI monthly sectoral deployment and NBFC credit release, CRIF/CIBIL delinquency, MFIN Micrometer, CP/NCD spreads. Capital markets: AMFI monthly note (AUM, SIP, folios), NSE/BSE monthly turnover, CDSL/NSDL accounts. Power: Grid-India daily PSP report (peak demand), CEA monthly generation and daily coal stock, IEX daily prices, MNRE capacity. Cement and steel: eight core industries index (monthly), JPC steel consumption, dealer price checks, China NBS exports, SGX iron ore. Capex: CGA monthly central capex, RBI OBICUS utilisation, IIP capital goods, CMIE project announcements. Consumption: GST collections (monthly, 1st of the month), NielsenIQ quarterly FMCG, CPI food, RBI consumer confidence, credit card spends, e-way bills. Real estate: ANAROCK/PropEquity quarterly, Knight Frank Mumbai registrations. Pharma: USFDA warning letters, 483s and import alerts, AIOCD monthly IPM growth. Defence: PIB DAC AoN releases and MoD contract signings. IT: Accenture results, which come about 3 weeks earlier, plus Naukri JobSpeak. Trap: mixing wholesale and retail, and failing to adjust for festival-calendar shifts. Oct 2026 FADA retail fell 14–28% only because Diwali moved into November, while SIAM wholesale rose 12–16%. **lesson:** Track one leading series per sector you own; always compare retail vs wholesale and adjust for calendar shifts. **example_nov_2026:** Oct 2026: SIAM PV +12.4%, 2W +16.1% vs FADA PV −14.2%, 2W −28.4% (Diwali shift). `event:india-modi-rally-2014` | confidence: **unverified** | tags: india, policy, rerating, smallcap, cyclical

From the taper-tantrum low (Sensex ~18,000, Aug-Sept 2013) the market re-rated on expectations of a decisive BJP win: Nifty crossed 7,000 around exit polls (May 2014) and the Sensex touched 25,000 intraday on results day, 16 May 2014; the Sensex then peaked near ~30,000 intraday in March 2015 (levels from memory). Calendar 2014 returns (from memory, unverified): Sensex ~+30%, BSE Midcap ~+55%, BSE Smallcap ~+69% - small caps led strongly. Leaders: PSU banks, capital goods, infra, cyclicals, mid/small caps that had been most beaten down; laggards: defensives (FMCG, pharma) on a relative basis. Valuation: Sensex P/E re-rated from ~15-16x to ~19-20x as earnings stayed flat - the move was hope. What followed: earnings disappointed for years (FY15-FY20 Nifty EPS growth was weak), the RBI's 2015 asset-quality review exposed PSU bank NPAs, and the Sensex fell ~25% to ~22,500 by Feb 2016. Signal visible at the time: the rally was P/E-driven with no earnings upgrades, and PSU banks rallied while stressed loans rose. Lesson: political change can trigger a sharp rerating from depressed valuations - the best returns came from buying the despair of 2013, not the euphoria of 2014-15; ratings without earnings fade.

`case_study:apl-apollo-2009-2026` · tickers: APLAPOLLO · confidence: verified

Split-adjusted ₹3.22 (Mar 2009) → ₹2,148 on 19 Nov 2026 ≈670x (ATH ₹2,270, Sep 2026). Twin engine: P/E 5.0 → 45.5 (9x) × implied EPS ~73x. Drawdowns: −84% (2008–09, before), −40% (2013), −57% (Jan 2018–Feb 2019). Early signal: a 'commodity' steel-tube maker with only 5–8% operating margin but ROCE 20–32%, high asset turns and branded distribution. In 2016–17 it installed India's first Direct Forming Technology (DFT) lines (Hosur, Raipur), making new hollow sections that replace angles and channels in construction. Reported structural-tube share ~40% by FY20. Working capital financed by dealers ('growth doesn't cost a rupee', smallcase). In 2013 the stock was at P/E ~4–5. Investors who tracked volumes and new-product share each quarter caught the 2014–2021 rerating. Not ended: FY26 PAT ₹1,203 cr (+59%), sales ₹23k cr, P/E ~45. 2018–19 −57% came from a steel-price slump and channel destocking, not a broken thesis. Lesson: low margins aren't the problem when asset turns are high and share is rising; screen on ROCE and volume growth, not OPM.

Key data: **start_year**: 2009; **end_year**: 2026; **start_price**: 3.22; **end_price**: 2148; **multiple**: ~670x; **pe_start**: 5.0; **pe_end**: 45.5; **eps_multiple_implied**: ~73x; **max_drawdown**: -57% (2018-19); **early_signals**: ROCE >20% at 5% margin; DFT tech 2016-17; ~40% share; **ended**: still running; **lesson**: ROCE + volume share > margin

body:
- **Rule:** cumulative exceptional charges over 5 years ÷ cumulative PAT. Above 10% means the "one-offs" are operating costs, so deduct their average from normalised earnings.
- One-off gains must also be stripped out.

**Worked example L: HUL FY26.**
- PAT went from 10,671 to **15,059 (+41%)**.
- In Q3 FY26 HUL recognised a one-time, **non-cash** exceptional gain of about ₹4,611 cr (standalone) on demerging its ice-cream business (Kwality Wall's). Under Ind AS 10 Appendix A, a distribution of non-cash assets to owners is measured at fair value. The same quarter carried a ₹576 cr exceptional charge for the new Labour Codes.
- Ex-gain PAT ≈ 15,059 − 4,611 ≈ **10,450**, i.e. **about −2% YoY**, not +41%.
- The effective tax rate fell from 26% to 17% because the gain is largely untaxed.
- *(Approximate: discontinued-operation profit and the consolidated and standalone treatments differ. Reconcile with the FY26 annual report.)*
- **Suzlon FY23** is the same pattern: other income of 2,739 against PBT of 2,892 (95%) in the debt-restructuring year. Without it, PBT is ₹153 cr.

- The sample comes from the *current* NSE list, so firms delisted before Nov-2026 are absent. Among the companies in it,
  no usable price series ends early (the fetch required ≥ 300 days and survival to today).
- **Size of the hole:** 1,508 unique companies filed Q3 FY19 results on NSE (Jan–Feb 2019; corporates-financial-results feed).
  **253 (16.8%) are no longer in the current equity list by symbol or ISIN.** A sample of the names shows a mix of failures
  and insolvencies (Punj Lloyd, Reliance Naval, Future Retail/Consumer, Lakshmi Vilas Bank, Ballarpur, SREI Infra, Naga
  Fertilisers) and mergers or delistings at a premium (Syndicate/Dena/Corporation Bank, Bharat Financial, Equitas Holdings, JMC
  Projects, JB Chemicals, GSPL). Many of the failures were below ₹500 cr when they died.
- **Direction of the bias.** Failures cluster in bad-earnings, bad-return firm-quarters, i.e., the *bottom* SUE quintile. Missing
  them makes the bottom quintile look better than it was, so **T−B is, if anything, understated**. For top-vs-controls both
  sides are survivors. The bias roughly cancels, unless delisted firms were disproportionately top-SUE with collapsing prices.
  That is implausible, and mergers (the other half) usually exit at a premium.
- **Rough bound (adverse):** suppose the missing firms are ~8% of event firm-quarters, spread evenly across SUE quintiles,
  with −20% 63d returns, and they are missing only on the event side (the controls do not include them either way). Then
  top-vs-controls falls ~1.8 pp, to ~+0.6% gross. A realistic mix (failures mostly bottom, mergers spread
  out) moves the long-only result by < ±0.5 pp.

body:
1. **Almost all stock-market wealth comes from very few stocks.** About 4% of US stocks
   created *all* the market's net wealth over 90 years. Most stocks lose to a bank FD.
   So we're hunting for rare winners, and most of our picks will be ordinary.
2. **F&O is a trap for individuals.** 88–93% of individual F&O traders in India lose
   money every year. In FY26, 82% were losing even *before* costs. Prop firms and
   foreign funds with algorithms took the other side. → **We don't do F&O.**
3. **Every legend had an unfair advantage, not just knowledge.**
   - Buffett: started at 11 in a market nobody studied; later used cheap insurance
     money (about 1.7x leverage); 99% of his wealth came after age 60–65.
   - Lynch: read ~700 annual reports and visited 200+ companies a year. Burned out at 46.
   - Damani: most of his wealth comes from *building* D-Mart, not trading.
   - Jhunjhunwala: started with "₹5,000" but borrowed his brother's clients' money; his
     biggest wealth came from a 1992 bet *against* the market; Titan was ~1/3 of his wealth.
4. **Myths we busted:** Titan wasn't bought at ₹3 (that's split-adjusted; he paid ₹30–50).
   The "Fidelity study of best investors being dead" never existed. Your Radico story
   was off: the 120 → 4,600 move started in **2016–17** (premium brands + debt falling),
   not from a 2008 UBL issue. UBL is a beer company.
5. **Multibaggers have "two engines":** profits grow *and* the market pays a higher P/E.
   Radico ≈ profit ×7.5 × P/E ×5 ≈ 38x.
6. **Winners fall hard along the way.** Amazon −94%, NVIDIA −50% twice, Radico −74%.
   You only get the reward if you can hold through that.
7. **Knowledge isn't the edge.** Millions read the same books. Edge = seeing what others
   don't, plus patience, plus never getting wiped out.
8. **AI doesn't pick winning stocks by itself.** AI trading contests mostly lost money;
   the oldest AI-run ETF trails the S&P 500. AI is great for *reading* and *checking*.
9. **Instant disqualifiers**, no matter how cheap the stock: promoter pledging shares,
   auditor qualifying the accounts, profits jumping with no real reason, growth funded
   by debt while cash flow is negative.
10. **Time and capital matter.** ₹25,000/month at 12% for 30 years ≈ ₹7.7 crore —
    more than ₹10,000/month at 15% (≈ ₹5.6 crore). Saving more beats chasing returns.

body:
Python 3.8+, standard library only. State is in `research_notes/Backtests/india_pead_live/` (git-tracked except
`.pxcache/`).

1. **Once (already done 2026-11-21 from the v2 caches):**
   `python3 tools/backtests/india_pead/live_tracker.py bootstrap <V1DIR> <V2DIR>`. This writes `universe.csv` (1,555
   names with shares), `eps_history.csv` (reported EPS per quarter and basis, 2019–Sep-2026), `sue_cutpoints.json`
   (fixed provisional quintile cuts) and an empty `predictions.csv`.
2. **Every weekday evening after about 20:00 IST** (results land through the evening):
   `python3 tools/backtests/india_pead/live_tracker.py update`. It reads the last 4 days of NSE result announcements
   (all companies, one call per day) and pulls each announcer's new integrated-filing XBRL (consolidated and
   standalone). It logs a row once the entry close exists, which is the close of the first trading day after the
   filing, so a row usually appears one run after the result. Expect about 1.5 s per company on result-heavy days
   (about 10–25 min on peak days). It checkpoints every 20 companies and is safe to re-run.
3. **Weekly (Saturday):** `live_tracker.py finalize` assigns in-quarter quintiles once a season closes.
   `live_tracker.py score` fills 21d and 63d outcomes vs size-matched controls (one Yahoo call per universe stock,
   cached 3 days, about 30 min) and rewrites `scorecard.md`.
4. **Pi crontab** (`crontab -e`; Pi clock in IST; repo at `~/fein`):
   ```
   15 20 * * 1-5  cd ~/fein && python3 tools/backtests/india_pead/live_tracker.py update   >> ~/pead_live.log 2>&1
   30 21 * * 6    cd ~/fein && python3 tools/backtests/india_pead/live_tracker.py finalize >> ~/pead_live.log 2>&1 && python3 tools/backtests/india_pead/live_tracker.py score >> ~/pead_live.log 2>&1
   45 22 * * 6    cd ~/fein && git add research_notes/Backtests/india_pead_live && git commit -qm "PEAD live: weekly update" && git push -q
   ```
   The first logged quarter is Q3 FY27 (31-Dec-2026), so rows start appearing about mid-January 2027. Earlier quarters
   are ignored unless `--first-qe` is passed. That is for testing only: 149 Sep-2026 rows were logged in a scratch
   directory on 2026-11-21 to check the code. Their SUE and basis matched `v2_events.py` exactly. 7 of 149 entered
   later than the backtest because their result-day announcement fell before the test window. The tracker now keeps
   `announcements.csv` permanently, so daily runs catch it.
5. **Caveats.** NSE endpoints change without notice. If `update` prints 0 companies on a results-season weekday,
   check `tools/nse_fetch.py` first. Yahoo symbol changes (renames) silently drop a name. New listings have no EPS
   history and enter after 8 quarters. The provisional quintile uses fixed cut points, so its bucket sizes will not be
   exactly 20%.

body:
The 2022–25 re-run has 14,624 events from 1,322 companies over 16 fiscal quarters; 79% use consolidated EPS. It uses
v1's method: the mean of the 16 quarterly values, a t-stat across quarters, and a bootstrap over quarters. Re-running
the events with full history left the fresh results identical (checked).

| Test (63d) | 2022–25 re-run | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| H1 top vs controls **net of 1%** | **+1.10% [−0.07, +2.18], t 1.88** (gross +2.10%, t 3.59) | **Does NOT replicate.** Same story as v1 and as 2026 |
| H2 contrast up − down (replication only) | **+3.02% [+1.50, +4.51], t 3.79**; filtered top net of 1% +2.32% (t 3.29) | Strong in 2022–25, the same data where v1 found it. **Failed on fresh 2026 data, so not supported** |
| H3 bottom vs controls | **−2.32% [−3.40, −1.23], t −4.11** | Replicates |
| H4 tertiles (exploratory): top vs controls / T−B | small +3.11% / +5.31%; mid +2.74% / **+5.86%**; large +1.29% / +2.95% | Mid is strongest on T−B in 2022–25 (v1 pattern), weakest in 2026 → **unstable** |

**Final verdicts.**
- **H1 not supported.** It fails on fresh data and in the re-run.
- **H2 not supported.** It replicates in-sample only and fails out of sample.
- **H3 supported.** It holds on fresh data and in the re-run.
- **H4 unstable** (exploratory).

Context (exploratory):
- T−B 63d is +4.33% (t 4.34). All events vs controls is +0.20%, so the controls are calibrated.
- Event-level top net of 1% is +1.00% (t 2.30, clustered by week over 127 weeks).
- 126d: top net of 1% +2.29% (t 2.80). This was not the primary horizon, as in v1.
- **2025 was weak on both legs** (event level, 63d: top +0.24%, bottom −0.55%; neither significant). 2026 recovered
  (+2.41% / −2.73%). This looks like a weak year, not a decay trend, but it is one more reason to run the live test.
